definition: Reheating already-hot condensed water back into steam takes far less energy than heating cold water from scratch, so most of a steam turbine's fuel consumption occurs during startup rather than continuous running.
core_idea: Because a cold start is the most fuel-intensive part of operating a steam turbine, plant operators often find it cheaper to keep a unit running — even accepting a loss during low-demand periods — than to shut down and later restart it.
key_points: Boiling water that is already near its boiling point requires much less added heat than boiling cold water
Startup/heat-up is the most fuel-consuming phase of steam turbine operation
Operators may choose to run at a loss during low-demand periods specifically to avoid cold-start costs
relationships: Related to must-run/unit-commitment behavior in generation fleets
trading_implications: Helps explain why some steam-turbine generators are willing to run through periods of low or negative prices rather than cycle off
caveats: A generator accepting a short-term loss isn't necessarily behaving irrationally — it can be avoiding a costlier cold restart
